intro: A 321 m sail of Teflon-coated fiberglass off Jumeirah Beach. Opened in 1999 as the world's tallest hotel, the Burj Al Arab became the symbol of Dubai's luxury pivot. Officially 5-star deluxe. Never seven-star.

sections.alt: Burj Al Arab sail profile seen from the beach
sections.body: The hotel was commissioned to become Dubai's symbolic icon. British multidisciplinary consultancy Atkins designed it, led by architect Tom Wright, who created the signature translucent fiberglass facade: a shield against the desert sun by day and an illumination screen by night. Design and construction were managed by Canadian engineer Rick Gregory, construction was managed by David Kirby, the interior is by British-Chinese designer Khuan Chew, and the helipad was designed by Irish architect Rebecca Gernon. Main contractors were Murray & Roberts/Concor of South Africa and Al Habtoor Engineering. The project cost about US$1 billion. One reading of this: the "symbolic icon" intent is documented; reading the building as the symbol of Dubai's late-1990s pivot from oil to luxury tourism is the researcher's framing, not a sourced claim.
sections.caption: The sail profile from the beach: the dhow-sail shape is the building's documented design intent.
sections.credit: Heba Hashem, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: An icon, commissioned

sections.alt: Burj Al Arab seen from the sea
sections.body: The beachfront site was previously called Chicago Beach, named for the Chicago Bridge & Iron Company, which once welded giant floating oil-storage tanks, locally called Kazzans, there. The former Chicago Beach Hotel was demolished during construction. The artificial island rises about 7.5 m above the waves in about 7.5 m of water, 280 m offshore of Jumeirah Beach, connected to the mainland by a private curving bridge. Its foundations: 230 concrete piles driven about 40 m into sand and silt, gaining stability from skin friction rather than bedrock, plus a surface layer of boulders wrapped in a concrete honeycomb wave-protection pattern. Island reclamation took about three years from 1994; the building itself took under three years. Up to 2,000 construction workers were on site at peak.
sections.caption: The hotel on its artificial island, 280 m offshore, joined to the mainland by a private curving bridge.
sections.credit: Marco Becerra, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: The island

sections.body: Two wings spread in a V to form a vast mast, with the space between enclosed as a 180 m tall atrium. A steel exoskeleton wraps a reinforced-concrete inner tower; the biggest truss is 85 m long and weighs 165 tonnes. Five-tonne hanging weights act as tuned dampers; maximum sway at the top of the accommodation is 300 mm. The front of the building is closed by a double-skinned Teflon-coated woven glass-fiber sail: two layers, a 50 cm air gap, twelve individually tensioned vertical panels, translucent by day and a projection screen at night. The V of the wings continues upward as a 60 m steel mast; accommodation tops out about 190 m above the island, the mast reaching 321 m. Materials: 70,000 m3 of concrete and 9,000 tonnes of steel, with 1,790 sq ft of 24-carat gold leaf in the interior. Thirty-nine percent of the building's height is non-occupiable space.
sections.heading: The sail and the mast

sections.body: The hotel is officially rated 5-star deluxe, the highest rating of both Forbes Travel Guide and Dubai DET. The "seven-star" label came from a British journalist who visited on a pre-opening tour and described it as beyond anything she had seen. A Jumeirah Group spokesperson said: "There's not a lot we can do to stop it. We've never used it in our advertising." The persistent, officially disavowed label became part of the building's mythology: a symbol of excess that critics called "a monument to the triumph of money over practicality," in Salma Samar Damluji's phrase from The Architecture of the U.A.E.
sections.heading: The seven-star myth

sections.body: The cantilevered helipad near the roof at 210 m, on the 28th floor, was designed by Irish architect Rebecca Gernon and rated for a 7.5-tonne helicopter. It received the UAE's first helipad license from the General Civil Aviation Authority in 2014. Its stunt history: a 2005 exhibition tennis match between Roger Federer and Andre Agassi, staged for the Dubai Duty Free Men's Open; Tiger Woods teeing off from it; Rory McIlroy, as Jumeirah's global ambassador, hitting golf balls off it in December 2011; David Coulthard doing donuts in a Red Bull F1 car in 2013 after the team's fourth consecutive championship; skydiver Nasser Al Neyadi landing on it; and, in 2017, Nick Jacobsen's record kiteboard jump from the helipad, 210 m above the water, the highest kiteboarding jump on record, smashing his own 90 m record.
sections.caption: The sail at sunset; the helipad cantilevers from the mast near the roof at 210 m.
sections.credit: Farrah Zakir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: The helipad stage

sections.body: The named spaces carry the building's meaning. Al Muntaha, "The Ultimate," is the restaurant 200 m above the sea, cantilevered 27 m out from the structure on a 1.7 m deep truss, with the Skyview Bar alongside. Al Mahara, "Oyster," is the seafood restaurant built around a 990,000-litre seawater aquarium behind 18 cm acrylic glass, reached through a simulated submarine voyage. The atrium's Sahn Eddar lounge, the Talise Spa, and four pools complete the venue set. All 202 suites are duplexes: the smallest is 170 m2, and the 780 m2 Royal Suite was billed at US$24,000 per night in 2012.
sections.heading: Named spaces

sections.body: In February 2026 the hotel was damaged and set on fire by debris from an intercepted drone during the 2026 Israeli-United States strikes on Iran; the fire was confined to the facade and put out shortly after. In April 2026 Jumeirah announced the hotel's first major restoration, expected to last about 18 months, with the interior to be made more modern while keeping its original look. Wikipedia lists the building's status as "Under Renovation." The only earlier physical expansion was the 2016 North Deck: the island was extended about 328 ft into the Gulf, adding an outdoor terrace, pools, and restaurant.
sections.heading: Damage and restoration
In the cultural conversation
sections.body: The hotel's screen life is thin; its defining cultural image is a sporting stunt. On 22 February 2005 Roger Federer and Andre Agassi played a 20-minute exhibition on the hotel's helipad, 210 meters above the Gulf, ahead of the Dubai Duty Free tournament. The ATP lists the match among 50 game-changing moments of the past 50 years, and it remains the single most reproduced image of the building. The hotel has no painting tradition; its visual culture lives in photography, advertising, and television.
